papers.abstract: With the emergence of radiotheranostics, radiation oncology practices are adapting to offer new radiopharmaceutical therapies (RPTs), while qualified medical physicists (QMPs) support these programs. However, RPT-specific medical physics training is variable, and heavily dependent on the clinical setting. QMPs may therefore be tasked with supporting RPT programs without adequate training in the subject matter. In 2025, the Nuclear Oncology Division of the Department of Radiation Oncology at Willis Knighton Cancer Center launched a first-of-kind, one-year Nuclear Oncology Physics Fellowship. Here, we detail our program structure and provide a framework for further expansion of nuclear oncology medical physics training. The fellowship is offered in partnership with three institutions: a large, tertiary community cancer center (hub site), a radiopharmaceutical research institution encompassing GMP isotope and radiopharmaceutical production and clinical and pre-clinical imaging, and a medical physics consulting group. The curriculum is split into twelve rotations covering the core competencies outlined by major certifying bodies. Primary mentors hold board certifications in diagnostic, nuclear medicine, or therapeutic medical physics. The fellowship may be completed before or after physics residency training, and culminates in a final project, in which the trainee designs a mock theranostics department. The program was verified to meet current training requirements for board certification in nuclear medicine physics. At the time of writing, the program enrolled its first fellow (pre-residency) and recruited its second trainee (post-residency). The fellowship provides a pathway for QMPs to gain the necessary training to support new theranostics programs. The curriculum may be adapted to accommodate the interests of each trainee and extended to support individuals in other crucial professions within the theranostics space. Future development of RPT-specific training guidelines may influence adjustments to the curriculum and certification processes; however, the current model provides a robust template for necessary QMP training.

papers.abstract: To assess the global and country-level greenhouse gas emissions implications of external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) scale-up to 2050. We conducted a country-level, scenario-based study across 181 countries to estimate EBRT-associated greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 and project emissions to 2050 under utilisation benchmarks of 50% and 64%, uniform schedules of 25, 15, and 5 fractions per course, and prespecified income-stratified Moderate and Ambitious hypofractionation pathways. Country-specific utilisation was examined as an access-constrained sensitivity scenario. Across all scenarios, global EBRT-associated emissions increased from 2022 to 2050. With 25-fraction delivery, emissions rose from 43.02 to 67.94 MtCO2e under the 50% utilisation and from 55.06 to 86.96 MtCO2e under the 64% utilisation. Under the 50% benchmark, 15- and 5-fraction schedules reduced 2050 emissions to 40.76 and 13.59 MtCO2e, respectively. Emissions shifted towards middle-income settings: the high-income share declined from 42.9% to 36.5%, while the 10 countries with the largest modelled EBRT-associated emissions still accounted for 64.5% of global emissions in 2022 and 60.6% in 2050. Compared with a uniform 25-fraction baseline, the Moderate pathway reduced global emissions by 23.3% in 2022 and 21.9% in 2050, while the Ambitious pathway reduced emissions by 36.5% and 34.7%, respectively. The largest absolute reductions occurred in high-income and upper-middle-income settings. Global EBRT-associated emissions are projected to rise substantially by 2050. Clinically appropriate hypofractionation offers a high-leverage mitigation opportunity, with priorities differing between decarbonising established high-volume systems and embedding low-carbon delivery during capacity expansion.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: The differentiation of endometrial cancer from non-malignant endometrial findings remains clinically important. We evaluated serum human epididymis protein 4 (HE4), clinical and ultrasound features, and two published diagnostic models, the Risk of Endometrial Malignancy (REM) score and Model A. Methods: In this prospective cohort, 110 women with abnormal uterine bleeding and/or ultrasound abnormalities underwent HE4 testing, transvaginal ultrasonography, and hysteroscopy with histopathological assessment. Original univariable analyses were supplemented by reanalysis of the individual study records, including ROC metrics, paired comparisons of AUCs, and an exploratory logistic model adjusting for age and endometrial thickness. Results: Endometrial cancer was diagnosed in 18 women; 92 had non-malignant findings. Median HE4 was higher in the cancer group (118.35 versus 52.3 pmol/L; p < 0.001, as originally reported). The AUC (95% bootstrap CI) was 0.834 (0.686–0.951) for HE4, 0.905 (0.794–0.981) for REM, and 0.840 (0.702–0.948) for Model A. AUC differences were not statistically significant (paired DeLong tests, all p > 0.10). In an exploratory adjusted analysis, each doubling of HE4 was associated with higher odds of malignancy (adjusted OR 5.41; 95% CI 1.81–16.21; p = 0.0025). Conclusions: HE4 and both published models discriminated between malignant and non-malignant findings in this selected cohort. The findings are exploratory and require independent validation before clinical use.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Combining omics layers is widely expected to improve cancer drug response prediction, but this is rarely tested under family-wise error control or on an independent screen. We measured what somatic mutation and copy number data add to gene expression, and how well models transfer to unseen lineages and an external screen. Methods: We linked the Cancer Dependency Map transcriptomic, somatic mutation and copy number profiles to GDSC2 dose–response data for twelve mechanistically diverse anticancer compounds in 509 cell lines. Lineage-only, single-modality, early-fusion and stacked late-fusion gradient-boosting models were compared by repeated cross-validation (DeLong tests, Holm adjustment), leave-one-lineage-out transfer across eleven solid tumour histologies, and external validation on 77-163 held-out PRISM cell lines per compound. Results: Gene expression models outperformed tissue-of-origin baselines for all twelve agents (AUC 0.69–0.84; gains 0.024–0.169; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001 for seven drugs). Adding mutation and copy number data changed AUC by −0.015 to +0.035, and no per-drug gain survived multiplicity correction. Pooled across compounds, early fusion added 0.008 AUC (95% CI 0.000–0.016), a gain that fold-level re-analysis did not support. Mixed-lineage cross-validation exceeded leave-one-lineage-out AUC by a median of 0.030 (p = 0.0005). External PRISM AUCs ranged from 0.46 to 0.76 and followed the concordance between the two screens (Spearman rho = 0.72, p = 0.008). TreeSHAP attributions recovered known determinants, including SLFN11, TP53, BRAF, PIK3CA and downstream MAPK transcriptional effectors. Conclusions: In this twelve-drug panel, gene expression captured most of the predictable response variation. Accuracy fell on held-out lineages and on an independent screen, which sets empirical limits on how far these models can generalise.

papers.abstract: Background: Radiation segmentectomy (RS) is the selective trans-arterial delivery of an ablative dose of radiation to tumor-bearing hepatic segments, with the goal of complete tumor necrosis comparable to resection or thermal ablation. The technique was first described in patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). RS has since been applied to intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) and to liver metastases of diverse origin, including colorectal, neuroendocrine, breast and sarcoma primaries. Purpose: To synthesize the original-data evidence base for RS across tumor types, to demonstrate the impact of tumor vascularity on tumor-specific dosimetry methods, and to define where the evidence supports standardization of methodology. Findings: Evidence is strongest for HCC, where pathologic-explant studies tie ablative dose thresholds to complete pathologic necrosis and prospective and large-cohort data demonstrate high response rates and extended patient survival. For colorectal liver metastases, several studies have associated tumor absorbed dose with response and local control. A single study additionally suggests that the dose delivered to the peritumoral margin is associated with local tumor control, an interesting hypothesis that requires further prospective validation. Data in iCCA and neuroendocrine metastases support feasibility and durable responses. The first international dosimetry consensus for non-HCC indications appeared in 2025. Heterogeneity in dosimetry models, dose thresholds, patient selection, and outcome reporting limits cross-study pooling. Conclusions: RS serves as a potentially curative locoregional therapy for selected patients with early-stage HCC and represents a promising treatment option for non-HCC tumors, especially for those not amenable to resection or thermal ablation. Histology-specific dosimetry, prospective validation, especially in non-HCC disease, and consensus reporting standards are necessary.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Metronomic cyclophosphamide (MCP) is sometimes used for advanced soft-tissue sarcoma (STS) when standard therapies are unsuitable. We assessed its activity and safety in routine practice. Methods: This French three-center retrospective study included 60 adults with unresectable or metastatic STS who started MCP in 2008–2021. Patients received oral cyclophosphamide 50 mg twice daily on days 1–7 of 14-day cycles; 12 (20%) also received prednisolone during treatment weeks. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Results: Median age was 70 years; 55% had ECOG performance status 2–3. Median PFS and overall survival (OS) were 2.6 months (95% CI, 1.8–3.6) and 6.4 months (95% CI, 4.2–9.3), respectively. The objective response rate was 5.0% (3/60; exact 95% CI, 1.0–13.9%) and the disease control rate was 21.7% (13/60; exact 95% CI, 12.1–34.2%); ten patients (16.7%) were not radiologically evaluable. In 21 patients aged >65 years treated in the first- or second-line setting, median PFS and OS were 3.2 and 7.7 months. Treatment-related adverse events were documented in 16 patients (26.7%), with no grade ≥3 events recorded. Conclusions: Intermittent low-dose MCP showed limited antitumor activity but favorable clinician-documented short-term tolerability in this multicenter cohort. Alongside prospective evidence, the results do not support routine use in unselected patients. MCP may retain an individualized palliative role when established systemic therapy is unsuitable.

papers.abstract: Soft tissue sarcomas (STSs) are genetically complex mesenchymal tumors with limited therapeutic options. BRCA1-associated protein 1 (BAP1), a deubiquitinase, is a critical regulator of chromatin architecture, DNA repair, and cell cycle control. While BAP1 alterations are well-characterized in mesothelioma and uveal melanoma, their role in STS remains understudied. Increasing evidence shows BAP1 alterations are associated with STS. This review summarizes current evidence on BAP1 biology and its emerging significance in sarcoma. We discuss BAP1’s molecular functions, including its role in the Polycomb Repressive Deubiquitinase (PR-DUB) complex, and summarize recent findings implicating BAP1 loss in multiple subtypes of STS. We highlight mechanistic links between BAP1 deficiency, genomic instability, and tumor progression, and explore therapeutic implications such as polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1) inhibition and epigenetic modulation. Understanding BAP1-driven pathways in STS may uncover novel biomarkers and targeted strategies, addressing a critical unmet need in sarcoma management.

papers.abstract: Pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant therapy is associated with favorable outcomes in breast cancer, yet differences in response cannot be explained by immune-cell abundance alone. This review examines pCR and residual disease from a spatial perspective. An effective antitumor response requires coordinated immune recruitment, local activation and renewal, movement across tissue boundaries, contact with malignant cells, and maintenance of effector function. Disruption at any stage may preserve resistant tumor regions despite substantial overall immune infiltration. Current evidence indicates that immune-cell positioning, multicellular organization, and the spatial distribution of stromal, vascular, and metabolic constraints can provide information beyond conventional cell-density measurements. However, the strength and clinical meaning of these associations vary according to breast cancer subtype, treatment regimen, sampling time point, and analytical platform. Pretreatment tissue, early on-treatment samples, and surgical residual disease address distinct baseline response-associated, pharmacodynamic, and prognostic questions and should therefore be interpreted separately. Residual disease represents a treatment-selected ecosystem rather than simply a smaller version of the untreated tumor. We integrate available evidence into a time-resolved framework linking baseline spatial architecture, treatment-related remodeling, residual disease organization, and subsequent clinical outcome. Translation into clinical practice will require standardized spatial definitions and measurements, reproducible assessment of organized immune structures, subtype- and regimen-specific validation, and demonstration of added value beyond established pathological indicators. Spatially resolved analysis may improve understanding of heterogeneous neoadjuvant responses and support more precise post-treatment risk assessment.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Non-invasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features (NIFTP) was reclassified as a non-malignant entity in 2016 to reduce overtreatment. A proportion of NIFTP-containing glands nonetheless harbour a synchronous differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC). We quantified its prevalence and pathological profile and assessed whether routinely collected pre-operative variables identify affected patients. Methods: A multicentre retrospective cohort of 1185 adults with NIFTP confirmed at second histological review, operated on between 2017 and 2023 in 22 centres. The outcome was a synchronous DTC in the surgical specimen. A weighted random forest and an elastic-net logistic regression based on 13 pre-operative predictors were evaluated with 20-times repeated five-fold cross-validation, with all data-driven steps nested within training folds, and with leave-one-centre-out and temporal validation. Results: A synchronous DTC was present in 61 patients (5.1%; 95% CI 4.0–6.6; 6.2% after review of the stored reports), with marked between-centre variation (none recorded in eight centres). Fifty-eight carcinomas (95%) were pT1a; none had gross extra-thyroidal extension or nodal metastasis (nodes examined in 27 patients), and none met the 2025 American Thyroid Association criteria mandating a more extensive operation. No pre-operative variable differed between groups after multiplicity adjustment. The cross-validated AUROC was 0.56 (95% CI 0.47–0.65) for the random forest and 0.58 (0.48–0.67) for the elastic net; the within-centre concordance was 0.48 and the temporal-validation AUROC 0.39, and decision-curve analysis showed no net benefit over default strategies. Conclusions: About one in twenty NIFTP-containing specimens harbours a synchronous DTC, usually a low-risk papillary microcarcinoma. Routinely available pre-operative variables do not identify these patients; management should be guided by the pathology of the carcinoma itself.

papers.abstract: Cancer neuroscience now asks not only whether tumors contain nerves, but how neural architecture, neuronal and glial states, and neural output change through cancer evolution. This critical narrative review integrates evidence from precursor lesions, primary tumors, invasion, metastasis, and treatment-associated states, while distinguishing neural remodeling from axonogenesis, neurogenesis, perineural invasion, and direct synaptic integration. We compare trophic, axon-guidance, metabolic, extracellular-vesicle, stromal, and neuroimmune mechanisms and emphasize that the direction of neural effects depends on stage, neuronal subtype, receptor context, and tissue immunity. The review operationalizes the proposed neural microdomain as a spatially bounded, measurable unit linking neural identity and topology to neighboring tumor, immune, stromal, and vascular states. It also separates neural abundance, neural state, and neural activity, and applies a consistent evidence taxonomy spanning anatomical, molecular, preclinical functional, human observational, and interventional evidence. Recent reports involving treatment-associated remodeling, systemic circuits, metastatic adaptation, and neural biomarkers are treated as emerging or preclinical where appropriate. We provide practical criteria for microdomain measurement, patient-level quantitative analysis, controls for denervation-related confounding, and distinctions among prognostic, predictive, and response biomarkers. The central translational conclusion is that neural interventions should be stage- and circuit-specific, biomarker-supported, and designed to preserve essential physiological neural functions.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Respiratory viral infections occur within the same anatomical niche as lung cancer, yet how lung cancer cells respond to infection and how these responses influence antiviral and inflammatory signalling remain poorly understood. This study investigated innate immune responses to influenza A virus (IAV) infection across a panel of lung epithelial cell lines. Methods: Non-malignant bronchial epithelial and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines representing adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma were infected with IAV. Antiviral and inflammatory gene expression, viral RNA and protein detection, infection-induced cell death, pattern recognition receptor expression, and immune checkpoint ligand expression were assessed using molecular, biochemical and flow cytometric approaches. Interferon (IFN) receptor blockade and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species scavenging were used to investigate selected signalling mechanisms. Results: NSCLC cell lines exhibited heterogeneous innate immune responses to IAV infection, with differential regulation of RNA-sensing pathways and canonical antiviral signalling components. Although IFN responses were retained, NSCLC cells exhibited reduced infection-induced apoptosis and prolonged viral RNA and protein detection compared with non-malignant epithelial cells. IAV infection was also associated with changes in DNA-sensing receptor expression, including TLR9, and increased expression of the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1. Conclusions: These findings identify substantial cell line-associated heterogeneity in antiviral responses to IAV across lung epithelial cell lines, including NSCLC cells. The observed differences in viral RNA and protein detection, cell death responses and immune-modulatory signalling provide a framework for understanding how respiratory viral infections may interact with lung cancer cells to shape antiviral and inflammatory responses within the tumour environment.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Bone metastases arise within a specialized microenvironment in which tumor cells interact with skeletal, stromal, vascular, immune, and hematopoietic compartments. Radiotherapy therefore affects not only metastatic tumor cells but also the surrounding bone and marrow niches. This review examines radiation-induced remodeling of the bone metastatic and bone marrow microenvironments across external-beam radiotherapy (EBRT) and radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT). Methods: We performed a narrative synthesis of experimental and clinical studies addressing cellular radiosensitivity, skeletal and stromal remodeling, hematopoietic injury, vascular and immune responses, oxidative and metabolic stress, and spatial and temporal patterns of radiation delivery. Emerging transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, lipidomic, single-cell, and spatial approaches were also considered. Results: EBRT and RPT produce overlapping but biologically distinct perturbations because of differences in dose rate, exposure duration, particle range, target localization, microscopic energy deposition, and spatial dose heterogeneity. These differences can influence tumor control, resistance, bone remodeling, and marrow toxicity through effects on osteoblasts, osteoclasts, stromal and vascular cells, immune populations, and HSPCs. These issues are particularly relevant to metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancers, in which bone seeking and tumor targeting radiopharmaceuticals differentially irradiate cellular compartments within the same skeletal environment. Conclusions: Bone metastases should be viewed as part of a dynamic bone–tumor–marrow microenvironment. Integrating radiation biology, spatial dosimetry, and multi-omics may support more individualized treatment strategies that maximize tumor control while limiting skeletal and hematologic injury.

papers.abstract: Purpose: Patients undergoing phase I cancer therapies experience high symptom burden and complications that may lead to emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalizations. It is unclear whether remote symptom monitoring (RSM) reduces acute care utilization. We conducted a secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial to determine if incorporating RSM into specialist palliative care (SPC) would reduce ED visits/hospitalizations. Methods: Patients with advanced cancer undergoing phase I therapies were randomized to SPC alone or SPC+RSM. Primary outcomes were ED visit and hospitalization frequencies over 6 months. We also assessed presenting concern, presentation etiology, and potential avoidability with two independent reviewers. Results: Among 100 patients (mean age 56, 63% female, median survival 221 [95% CI 171, 271] days), 43 were in the SPC group and 57 were in the SPC+RSM group. A total of 22/43 (51%) SPC patients and 30/57 (53%) SPC+RSM patients had at least one ED visit over 6 months (p = 0.58), while 18/43 (42%) SPC patients and 21/57 (37%) had at least one hospitalization over 6 months (p = 0.56). The most common presenting symptoms were pain (ED 27%, hospitalizations 29%) and respiratory symptoms (ED 22%, hospitalization 22%). The main reasons for acute care encounters were disease progression (ED 49%, hospitalizations 58%) and acute complications (ED 26%, hospitalizations 28%). Only 4/84 (5%) ED visits and 0/57 (0%) of the hospitalizations were deemed avoidable. Conclusions: Acute care utilization was high in phase I patients. RSM did not reduce ED visits/hospitalizations, which were mostly unavoidable. Our findings highlight the need for novel strategies to support this population.

papers.abstract: Therapeutic resistance remains a major barrier to durable cancer control and is increasingly recognized as a dynamic process shaped not only by genetic evolution but also by metabolic adaptation. Nucleotide metabolism is uniquely positioned at this interface, supporting DNA and RNA synthesis while also regulating signaling, energy homeostasis, redox balance, genome maintenance, and cellular stress responses. In this Review, we examine emerging evidence that cancer cells in solid tumors adapt nucleotide metabolism in response to therapeutic pressure through coordinated remodeling of de novo biosynthesis, nucleotide salvage, metabolite transport, and pathway-specific feedback mechanisms. We discuss how cytotoxic chemotherapy, targeted therapies, immunotherapies, and radiation impose distinct but convergent pressures on nucleotide homeostasis and how restoration or redistribution of nucleotide pools can promote survival, DNA repair, persistent oncogenic signaling, and immune evasion. We further highlight the reciprocal relationship between oncogenic signaling and nucleotide metabolism, as well as the contribution of tumor suppressor loss and the tumor microenvironment to context-specific metabolic dependencies. Rather than functioning only as a biosynthetic requirement of proliferating cells, nucleotide metabolism emerges as a flexible stress-response network that can facilitate adaptation to cancer therapy. Defining the mechanisms that maintain nucleotide balance in resistant tumors may reveal therapeutically actionable dependencies and inform rational combination strategies designed to prevent or overcome treatment resistance.

papers.abstract: Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women globally, accounting for one in four cancer cases and one in six cancer deaths. Timely initiation of treatment after diagnosis is critical to improving survival outcomes. However, delays in treatment initiation remain widespread, influenced by health system constraints, socio-demographic factors, and the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite growing recognition of this issue, no prior study has comprehensively quantified global evidence on diagnosis-to-treatment delays in breast cancer. Our objective was to systematically review and synthesize global evidence on time to treatment initiation (TTI) among patients with breast cancer, and to estimate pooled mean delays and the proportion of patients experiencing delays at predefined cutoffs (30, 60, and 90 days). This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Four databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase) were searched from inception to October 15, 2025. Eligible observational studies reported TTI as mean/median days or as proportions of patients with delayed initiation. Data were pooled using DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models. Subgroup analyses were performed by publication period, WHO region, study setting, and World Bank income group. A sensitivity analysis excluded United States datasets. Risk of delay was compared by stage at diagnosis. Risk of bias was assessed with the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Sixty studies (analyzed as 62 datasets) involving 3644,548 breast cancer patients from 21 countries were included. The pooled mean TTI was 51.7 days (95% CI: 46.5-56.9; I² = 99.9%). At the 30-day cutoff, 37% (95% CI: 25-49%) of patients experienced delays; at 60 days, 17% (95% CI: 11-22%); and at 90 days, 4% (95% CI: 3-5%). The United States contributed 32 datasets and 70.1% of participants. Excluding these datasets raised the pooled mean TTI to 75.0 days (95% CI: 44.5-105.5). Mean TTI was 39.8 days in high-income countries and 79.7 days in low- and middle-income countries (p = 0.07). Delays beyond 90 days affected 2.6% and 26.5% of patients, respectively (p < 0.001). Stage at diagnosis was not associated with delay. Delays between diagnosis and treatment initiation are common, with more than one-third of patients waiting over 30 days. The pooled estimate reflects mainly high-income settings. Delays are longer, and very long delays more frequent, in low- and middle-income countries, where evidence remains sparse. Agreed TTI benchmarks, stronger oncology services, and more primary studies from low- and middle-income countries are priorities to close the cancer care gap.

papers.abstract: Off-label use of anticancer medicines is common. Investigator-initiated trials evaluating off-label indications often do not result in label expansion. Additionally, off-label use is often considered when approved treatments are lacking or exhausted. Such use may lead to uncertain efficacy and safety and poses reimbursement challenges. This study examines the Dutch framework to evaluate off-label indications for population-level reimbursement. We quantify national off-label oncology drug use and analyse its supporting evidence to identify clinical needs and support policy development. We identified reimbursable oncology indication-drug pairs (IDPs) using the World Health Organization Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification. Approved and off-label indications were mapped using European Medicines Agency marketing authorisations, European Society for Medical Oncology guidelines, medical literature, and the national medicines database. National 2023 health care registry data were analysed to quantify off-label prescribing and expenditure for high-cost oncology drugs. Evidence supporting selected off-label treatments was evaluated using public assessment reports and clinical guidelines. As of January 2025, 331 of 930 (35.6%) reimbursable oncology IDPs were off-label, mainly involving high-cost drugs (n = 299 of 331, 90.3%). Off-label treatments frequently involved chemotherapy, accounting for 67.1% (n = 163 of 331) of off-label IDPs. Targeted therapies comprised 32.9% (n = 109 of 331). For high-cost drugs, 24.4% (n = 41 238 of 169 043) of prescriptions were off-label in 2023, representing only 2.3% (€30.3 million of €1.3 billion) of total expenditure on these drugs. Targeted therapies posed the largest financial impact, representing 67.7% (€20.5 of €30.3 million) of off-label expenditure. The Dutch framework reimbursed off-label treatments meeting thresholds for clinical benefit. Frequently used off-label treatments were supported by strong evidence. Evidence levels varied for rarer indications. The high prevalence of off-label oncology treatments in The Netherlands underscores the importance of a framework to evaluate off-label indications for reimbursement, ensuring access to effective and financially sustainable treatments. It also highlights the need for policy reform to encourage regulatory approval.

papers.abstract: Chemoimmunotherapy has become the standard first-line treatment for de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (dmNPC). However, the role and optimal timing of locoregional radiotherapy in dmNPC in the chemoimmunotherapy era remain unclear. This study aims to evaluate whether salvage locoregional radiotherapy (SLRRT), deferred until locoregional progression in patients with well-controlled distant metastases, compromises survival compared with immediate locoregional radiotherapy (ILRRT) in responders to first-line chemoimmunotherapy. This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients with dmNPC who achieved a complete or partial response after first-line platinum-based chemotherapy combined with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 therapy. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS). Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to adjust for baseline characteristics. Survival outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analyses and a multivariate Cox regression model. A total of 439 patients were included, with a median follow-up of 35.0 months (interquartile range, 24.0-45.2). Of these, 331 patients were assigned to the ILRRT cohort and 108 to the SLRRT cohort. After IPTW adjustment, SLRRT was not associated with inferior OS compared with ILRRT [2-year OS, 97.4% versus 90.1%; hazard ratio (HR) 0.93, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.54-1.59, P = 0.78]. SLRRT was associated with worse locoregional control (HR 4.78, 95% CI 2.98-7.66, P < 0.001) but better distant control (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.95, P = 0.03). Radiotherapy-related adverse effects were substantially more frequent in the ILRRT cohort. Deferring SLRRT until locoregional progression did not compromise survival among responders to first-line chemoimmunotherapy. These findings support a response-adapted, de-escalated treatment strategy that may reduce treatment-related toxicities and improve quality of life without adversely affecting survival.

papers.abstract: Posterior lumbar plexus block provides reliable anesthesia but is technically challenging and associated with risks related to deep paraspinal needle placement. Existing anterior approaches provide variable lumbar plexus coverage, and the anatomical pathways by which newer iliopsoas-based techniques reach individual plexus branches remain incompletely defined. This feasibility study evaluated whether an anterior inferior, trans-psoas injection targeting the posterior epimysium of the psoas muscle could provide a direct anterior pathway toward the lumbar plexus. A cadaveric dye study was performed on four GreenMBalmed cadaver hips. Under ultrasound guidance in the supine position, 30 mL of 0.1% methylene blue was injected in a caudal-to-cranial trajectory along the posterior epimysium of the psoas. Layered dissections assessed dye spread relative to the psoas, thoracolumbar fascia, and lumbar plexus nerves. Cranial and anterior fascial spread was observed in all four hips, with dye tracking anterior to the quadratus lumborum and extending toward the 12th rib and perinephric region. Dense staining of the lateral femoral cutaneous and iliohypogastric nerves was seen in all hips. The femoral nerve demonstrated predominantly moderate staining, while obturator nerve involvement was variable. Minimal intramuscular staining of the psoas was observed, suggesting preferential spread along fascial planes. Anterior inferior injection along the posterior epimysium of the psoas produced spread toward lumbar plexus regions in all four hips, in this limited cadaveric sample, suggesting this plane warrants further investigation. Clinical studies are needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of this approach.

papers.abstract: Processed electroencephalography (pEEG) provides quantitative indices for monitoring anesthetic depth and is recommended in international guidelines. Prior meta-analyses have assessed EEG-guided anesthesia but none have evaluated available evidence stratified by pEEG technology. We performed a systematic literature review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials in adults undergoing surgical, endoscopic, or dental procedures comparing pEEG-guided with non-pEEG-guided anesthesia. Primary outcomes were anesthetic drug use (TIVA and volatile agents) and postoperative delirium (POD ≤10 days). Secondary outcomes were extubation time, wake-up time, time to orientation, and post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) length of stay. Searches (PubMed Central, MEDLINE) were conducted on 11 April 2025; the protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251067170). Random-effects models produced standardized mean differences (SMD), mean differences (MD), and risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence interval (CI). Eighty-seven RCTs (30,611 patients; 13,586 pEEG; 17,025 non-pEEG) were included. pEEG significantly reduced propofol use (SMD -0.42, 95% CI -0.74 to -0.10; p = 0.01) and volatile anesthetic use (SMD -1.27, 95% CI -1.88 to -0.66; p < 0.01). The risk of POD decreased by 27% (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.84; p < 0.01). Efficiency outcomes favored pEEG: extubation time (MD -2.90 min, 95% CI -3.64 to -2.16; p < 0.01), wake-up time (MD -1.83 min, 95% CI -2.42 to -1.25; p < 0.01), time to orientation (MD -4.11 min, 95% CI -6.99 to -1.23; p < 0.01), and PACU length of stay (MD -2.81 min, 95% CI -4.66 to -0.96; p < 0.01). Subgroup analyses suggested benefits were most consistently observed for BIS; estimates for Entropy and SEDLine were less precise due to fewer studies. Heterogeneity was substantial for several outcomes. Across 87 RCTs, pEEG-guided monitoring utilizing multiple device types improved perioperative efficiency and reduced POD compared with not using pEEG. Evidence is strongest for BIS; further well-reported trials are needed to delineate device-specific effects.

papers.abstract: Chimeric RNAs are a class of molecules defined as RNA transcripts containing genetic information for multiple genes. While their expression patterns across tissue types and disease states have been well documented, the biological function of these transcripts remains poorly understood. In this study, we developed an integrative prediction pipeline to establish an atlas of 569,640 chimeric RNAs across 1019 cancer cell lines. Leveraging this resource, we performed a systematic functional dependency screen by integrating our predictions with perturbation datasets from The Cancer Dependency Map project. This approach moves beyond prediction to identifying high-confidence functional chimeric RNAs essential for cellular processes, including a subset of recurrent chimeric transcripts generated by cis-splicing of adjacent genes. We demonstrate that depletion of selected candidate chimeras disrupts cell cycle progression and cellular fitness and that these transcripts are frequently dysregulated in primary breast tumors. Together, these results demonstrate that chimeric RNAs constitute a previously underappreciated layer of gene expression, expanding the functional genome beyond conventional genetics.

papers.abstract: Sprouting angiogenesis is critical for embryogenesis, wound healing, and tumor growth. Here, we show that the liquid crystal framework, which has recently been leveraged to study various morphogenetic events, provides unique insight into angiogenic sprouting. In response to vascular endothelial growth factor, a potent proangiogenic factor, endothelial cells cultured on the surfaces of soft collagen hydrogels form elongated cell streams that coexist with more polygonal cell regions. Angiogenic sprouting initiates preferentially at cell stream tips, where nematic order gradients are most pronounced. We demonstrate that cell streams are associated with large traction forces that lead to three-dimensional deformations of the underlying hydrogel and that stream formation results from a delicate balance between microtubule polymerization and actomyosin contractility. Last, we show that active control of nematic order allows modulation of sprout formation, highlighting the key role of endothelial cell orientation gradients in angiogenic sprouting and paving the way for new therapeutic avenues.

papers.abstract: Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) are constitutively active in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) cells. Here, we investigated whether these cells could still respond to hypoxia independently of canonical HIF activation. We found that hypoxia provokes a NADH reductive stress that attenuates lactate release when the supply of extracellular pyruvate becomes limited, a response that was restored by the ectopic expression of the cytosolic and mitochondria-targeted NADH oxidase (LbNOX). Suppression of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (mtETC) alone is sufficient to attenuate glycolytic flux when extracellular pyruvate is limited, a situation consistent with metabolomic data from human ccRCCs. Furthermore, this response can be mimicked by pharmacological or genetic inhibition of mitochondrial complex IV (CIV) activity and restored by the mitochondrial-targeted alternative oxidase (AOX). Therefore, our data suggest that cells can respond to low oxygen tension through a mitochondrial-dependent elevation of NADH/NAD+, resulting in the suppression of glycolysis when pyruvate availability is compromised.

papers.abstract: The assembly of cellular spheroids into spatially organized assembloids represents a transformative paradigm for modeling complex biological systems. However, the lack of standardized fabrication strategies fundamentally limits the precision and reproducibility of these models, hindering their widespread application. Here, we present a robotic micromanipulation platform-Fluid-Driven Tweezer with Visual Servo Control (FDT-VSC). By integrating multidimensional visual perception with microfluidic control, our system enables the gentle and programmable assembly of diverse cellular spheroids. Leveraging this platform, we achieve the bottom-up construction of structurally defined, heterogeneous multicellular tissues, and the programmed orchestration of multilineage models that recapitulate the complex microenvironments of early organogenesis. Crucially, the system improves consistency during the scalable fabrication of tumor-stroma assembloids, supporting reliable drug screening. These results demonstrate that FDT-VSC advances assembloid-based applications across modular tissue engineering, developmental biology, and drug discovery.

papers.abstract: Aberrant glutamine metabolism undermines the efficacy of cancer radiotherapy (RT) by promoting DNA repair, increasing oxygen consumption, and imposing metabolic stress that compromises the viability and function of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs). Here, we report a mitochondria-enriched, metabolism-regulating monolayered metal-organic framework (MOF) nanoplatform, Hf-Ir/DON, constructed by incorporating the glutamine antagonist 6-diazo-5-oxo-l-norleucine (DON) into a radiosensitizing hafnium-iridium (Hf-Ir) MOF to inhibit glutaminolysis. This design markedly sensitizes tumor cells to RT and, upon x-ray irradiation, enables mitochondria-targeted RT-radiodynamic therapy with substantially enhanced reactive oxygen species accumulation. The resulting oxidative stress induces extensive DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and immunogenic tumor cell pyroptosis. Concurrently, Hf-Ir/DON alleviates metabolic constraints on activated T cells, preserving CTL viability while sustaining effector and memory functions. In a murine colon cancer model, low-dose RT combined with Hf-Ir/DON achieved >95% tumor growth inhibition. Further combination with anti-PD-L1 therapy induced regression of bilateral triple-negative breast tumors and prevented lung metastasis. These results establish a radiometabolic MOF nanoplatform that potentiates RT while promoting durable antitumor immunity.

papers.abstract: Adolescent and young adult (AYA) oncology has emerged as a distinct field in response to persistent disparities in outcomes among patients aged 15-39 years, who often experience fragmented care across pediatric and adult systems. For surgeons, these challenges are especially relevant because biopsy, resection, metastatic disease management, fertility-preservation procedures, and survivorship planning frequently hinge on the surgical pathway through which patients enter cancer care. This review summarizes the epidemiology, systems-level barriers, biologic considerations, and supportive care priorities that define comprehensive AYA surgical oncology care. AYA malignancies encompass both pediatric-type tumors and adult-onset carcinomas, creating ambiguity in referral patterns, trial access, and treatment setting. Current evidence supports care at specialized or hybrid AYA-focused centers that integrate pediatric and adult expertise, multidisciplinary coordination, psychosocial support, fertility counseling, and survivorship services. However, major gaps remain, including low clinical trial enrollment, inconsistent access to age-appropriate supportive care, financial toxicity, and inadequate coordination of fertility preservation and long-term follow-up. Emerging data also suggest meaningful age-associated differences in tumor biology across reinforcing the need for developmentally and biologically informed treatment planning. Given the rarity and heterogeneity of AYA malignancies, age-informed care pathways built on structured collaboration between pediatric and adult surgeons offer a realistic and scalable model to align surgical decision-making with the developmental and oncologic needs of this population.

papers.abstract: Regulatory T cell (Treg) accumulation within the tumor microenvironment is a major contributor to immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance. However, the metabolic signals orchestrating Treg lineage commitment remain poorly defined. We identify that the oxysterol 7α,25-dihydroxycholesterol (7α,25-OHC), produced by Vimentin+ stromal cells, acts through GPR183 to promote Treg differentiation and suppressive identity. In patients with gastric cancer (GC), GPR183+ Treg infiltration correlates with advanced disease and poor survival. In syngeneic tumor models, conditional GPR183 deletion, specifically in CD4+ T cells or Treg cells, demonstrates its cell-intrinsic requirement for high-cholesterol-diet-induced Treg expansion and tumor growth, thereby abrogating immune evasion and restoring CD8+ T cell effector function. Mechanistically, 7α,25-OHC-GPR183 signaling activates the AXL-JAK2-STAT5 pathway to reinforce Foxp3 expression. Last, GPR183 antagonism modestly enhances anti-PD-1 efficacy in a model-dependent manner and prevents therapy-induced Treg expansion. These findings identify the 7α,25-OHC-GPR183-AXL axis as a potential metabolic checkpoint linking cholesterol metabolism to immune suppression, suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy to enhance antitumor immunity.

papers.abstract: Epithelial surfaces are the primary sites of lytic herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) infection following initial exposure or reactivation from latency. To model this complex environment, we used human hair-bearing skin organoids and combined single-cell spatial transcriptomics with imaging to map viral spread and host responses across skin architecture. Our data suggest delayed progression of the HSV-1 life cycle in epidermal keratinocytes and hair follicle cells compared to the dermis. Infection triggered spatially organized host responses, including induction of IER3 in papillary fibroblasts. In basal keratinocytes, IRF3 was up-regulated in both infected and neighboring uninfected cells, consistent with paracrine activation of antiviral signaling. Inflammatory responses were compartmentalized in a cell type-specific manner, with TNFSF9 (4-1BBL) induced in papillary fibroblasts and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) induced in keratinocytes. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays confirmed secretion of these cytokines and the TNF-α-responsive chemokines CXCL2 and CXCL10. CXCL2 expression was enriched in cells adjacent to TNF-α-expressing cells, highlighting spatial coordination of inflammatory signaling. While interferon-β reduced viral replication, TNF-α and 4-1BBL did not, suggesting that their primary role is to orchestrate immune cell recruitment and activation. These findings establish human hair-bearing skin organoids as a physiologically relevant model for investigating spatial host-HSV-1 interactions.

papers.abstract: PDS5A, a cohesin regulatory subunit, and topoisomerase IIB (TOP2B), an enzyme resolving DNA topological problems, interact with CTCF and regulate transcription and genome organization. We ascertained that PDS5A and TOP2B are recruited to CTCF-bound chromatin cooperatively and that catalytically active TOP2B increases PDS5A occupancy genome wide. Notably, the amino-terminal 95 to 116 amino acids of CTCF interacts with PDS5A, giving rise to CTCF-PDS5A-TOP2B interaction in vitro and to PDS5A chromatin enrichment via active TOP2B in vivo. PDS5A-TOP2B function together in moderating the resultant gene expression and genome organization. Loss of CTCF (95 to 116 amino acids) led to dysregulated gene expression and mildly reduced chromatin loops. In gliomas, PDS5A and TOP2B expression levels vary, but correlate, contributing to distinctive gene expression patterns. Inducible PDS5A knockdown led to reduced TOP2B occupancy and altered gene expression. Furthermore, PDS5A mediated sensitivity to TOP2 cancer drugs in glioma cells. This functional interaction between PDS5A and TOP2B at CTCF boundaries expands upon the mechanisms affecting gene regulation through genome organization, with implications for glioma therapeutics.

papers.abstract: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue-compatible spatial transcriptomics (ST) is transforming biology and histopathology, but achieving high sensitivity, genome-wide coverage, single-cell resolution, and researcher accessibility remains challenging. To address these challenges, we here present a dendrimeric DNA coordinate barcoding design for FFPE tissue-adapted spatial RNA sequencing (Decoder-FFPE-seq) by integrating RNA-to-DNA probe conversion with blotting-assisted barcoding. Decoder-FFPE-seq provides single-cell resolution with a >2.6-fold sensitivity increase in whole-transcriptome mouse brain and archived human sample profiling over existing platforms, resolving potential cellular identity of low-abundance genes, finer tissue architecture, and capturing an epithelial-mesenchymal transition-associated signature for prognostic value. With expanded probe libraries, Decoder-FFPE-seq captures long noncoding and viral RNAs, revealing their spatial coregulatory networks with messenger RNAs in oral squamous cell carcinomas (OSCCs). In an OSCC immunotherapy cohort, two CD8+ T cell subpopulations were respectively identified in pre- and postchemoimmunotherapy samples, potentially linked to treatment response. Decoder-FFPE-seq establishes a robust, high-resolution, and accessible framework for sensitive ST profiling of archival tissues in fundamental and translational studies.

papers.abstract: Whole-genome doubling (WGD) occurs frequently in human cancer and influences tumor evolution, metastasis, and treatment response. Here, we integrate bulk, single-cell, and spatial data to dissect the subclonal dynamics of WGD. Single-cell data analysis shows that WGD cells are prevalent even in tumors that are classified as non-WGD (nWGD). WGD subclones actively acquire somatic copy number alterations as they expand, suggesting ongoing evolution. We developed and rigorously validated a gene expression-based method, WAGES, to map WGD cell clonal fraction in bulk tumors. Applying WAGES to nWGD tumors, we reveal genomic correlates including TP53 mutations and chromosomal instability that are consistent with the presence of WGD subclones. Clinically, WAGES scores are strongly correlated with tumor metastatic potential, response to treatments including chemotherapy and immunotherapy, and patient prognosis. These findings reveal widespread WGD subclones in nWGD tumors and demonstrate their substantial impact on cancer evolution and therapeutic outcomes.

papers.abstract: Abstract T cells initiate anticancer immune responses at an early stage of tumorigenesis, thus enabling dynamic monitoring of peripheral blood T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire changes as a promising strategy for early cancer detection. However, the current TCR-based cancer detection methods focus on limited high-frequency TCRs instead of repertoire-scale representation, overlooking numerous crucial cancer-associated TCRs (caTCR). Herein, we developed ScanTCR, a computational framework for early cancer detection that introduces a reference-guided repertoire-scale encoding method capable of incorporating all TCRs. ScanTCR exhibited remarkable precision in distinguishing patients with cancer from noncancer individuals using peripheral blood TCRs. In a pan-cancer analysis encompassing seven cancer types, ScanTCR demonstrated robust performance in detecting both cancer types included in the training data and unseen cancer types, surpassing state-of-the-art TCR-based methods. Furthermore, ScanTCR identified caTCRs in which corresponding T cells exhibit enhanced cellular immune capacity. Collectively, this work proposes a TCR-based approach enabling repertoire-scale representation of immune receptors for noninvasive early cancer detection. Significance: Overcoming limitations of current methods that favor high-frequency cancer-associated T-cell receptors, repertoire-scale profiling preserves all sequences for accurate cancer detection, supporting the potential of this approach for early-stage cancer diagnostics.

papers.abstract: Abstract Cellular senescence contributes dynamically to fibrosis and cancer depending on the senescent cell type and its tissue remodeling senescence-associated secretory phenotype; however, current senotherapies lack specificity in targeting pathogenic senescent cells and have limiting toxicities. In a recent issue of Science, Hinterleitner and colleagues designed P-selectin-directed nanoparticles (SMNPs) capable of delivering senotherapies specifically to pathogenic P-selectin+ senescent macrophages in fibrotic tissues while preventing uptake in beneficial senescent endothelial cells. Precision targeting by SMNPs resolved fibrosis and restored organ function in the lung and liver and minimized senotherapeutic toxicity in mice. In tumor models, SMNP targeting of this small senescent macrophage subset was sufficient to overcome fibrosis-mediated immune exclusion and sensitize liver and lung cancers to T cell-directed immunotherapy. P-selectin+ macrophages with senescent features were also enriched in fibrotic human tissues and treatment-refractory cancer patient samples. Overall, this study provides a platform for reducing the toxicity and enhancing the specificity of senotherapies necessary to advance their clinical development for treating chronic disease.

papers.abstract: Abstract Although chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)–engineered T- and NK-cell therapies have revolutionized hematologic malignancy treatment, translating this success to solid tumors remains a persistent challenge. In this study, we demonstrated a stromal-associated metabolic mechanism in which cancer-associated fibroblasts and macrophage-associated populations in gastrointestinal cancers contribute to CAR loss through CYP27A1-derived 27-hydroxycholesterol (27HC). 27HC triggered membrane cholesterol depletion, destabilizing lipid rafts and promoting the release of full-length CAR in ARF6+CD81+ microvesicle–enriched fractions. NK92 cells chronically exposed to sublethal 27HC adapted to this stress via an AKT–FOXO1–insulin receptor (INSR) signaling cascade that restores cholesterol biosynthesis. Capitalizing on this mechanism, “metabolically armored” INSR-overexpressing CAR-NK92 and primary CAR-T cells were engineered, which stabilized lipid rafts, preserved CAR expression, and improved antitumor activity in patient-derived organoids, precision-cut tumor slices, and xenografts. Collectively, these findings identify a stromal-mediated metabolic immune evasion pathway in gastrointestinal tumors, uncovering a potential strategy to potentiate CAR-engineered therapies. Significance: Stromal 27HC promotes cholesterol loss and CAR shedding, which can be overcome with INSR armoring to preserve cholesterol homeostasis and improve CAR-NK and CAR-T cell activity in gastrointestinal tumor models.

papers.abstract: Abstract Clinical outcomes are often suboptimal in patients with colorectal cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC). A key determinant of the response to NAC is the functional state of tumor-infiltrating immune cells. Understanding how NAC reshapes the immunologic landscape will be essential for refining patient stratification and identifying effective combination treatment strategies. In this study, we analyzed paired samples before and after NAC treatment by single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), revealing that NAC treatment significantly reshaped the immune microenvironment. Tumors from NAC nonresponders featured increased immunosuppressive M2-like macrophage infiltration, which correlated with elevated phosphatidylserine-specific phospholipase A1 (PLA1A). Mechanistically, PLA1A hydrolyzed phosphatidylserine (PS) exposed by chemotherapy to elevate lysophosphatidylserine (LysoPS), which activated the P2ry10 receptor and downstream signaling to promote M2-like macrophage polarization. Importantly, pharmacologic inhibition of PLA1A by cilengitide synergized with chemoimmunotherapy to suppress tumor progression in murine models. Clinically, high plasma PLA1A levels negatively correlated with responses to chemoimmunotherapy. Collectively, these findings reveal a chemotherapy-driven metabolic axis that induces an immunosuppressive milieu by increasing LysoPS release. This axis highlights PLA1A as a therapeutic target to mitigate immunosuppression and improve chemoimmunotherapy efficacy. Significance: Chemotherapy-resistant colorectal cancer elevates PLA1A to induce anti-inflammatory macrophage polarization, supporting the potential of PLA1A as a therapeutic target for enhancing chemoimmunotherapy efficacy and as a biomarker of treatment response.

papers.abstract: Abstract Fibroblast activation and extracellular matrix stiffening are hallmarks of the fibrotic tumor microenvironment. Fibrotic microenvironmental remodeling is also linked to immune exclusion and evasion, suggesting that common microenvironmental signals might coordinate both fibrotic and inflammatory outputs. In this study, we identified methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase 2 (MTHFD2) as a redox-sensitive metabolic regulator linking TGFβ-driven fibroblast activation to inflammatory signaling in lung adenocarcinoma. MTHFD2 was elevated in cancer-associated fibroblasts across multiple single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, and TGFβ induced MTHFD2 even under compliant matrix conditions, with matrix stiffening further enhancing its expression. Notably, although MTHFD2 knockdown suppressed both myofibroblastic and inflammatory programs, enforced expression was sufficient to drive inflammatory cytokine production even in the absence of TGFβ, and this response was further amplified by concomitant TGFβ signaling. These MTHFD2-mediated responses depended on redox perturbation rather than biosynthetic one-carbon metabolism, as they resisted formate supplementation but responded to pro-oxidants. Mechanistically, MTHFD2-driven redox imbalance promoted mitochondrial stress, cytosolic mitochondrial DNA accumulation, and activation of the cGAS–STING–NF-κB pathway, resulting in IL6 and IL8 production. Fibroblast-specific MTHFD2 knockdown suppressed paracrine programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) induction in tumor cells and inhibited tumor growth in vivo in an immune-dependent manner. Clinically, high stromal MTHFD2 correlated with epithelial PD-L1 expression and poor lung adenocarcinoma prognosis. Together, these findings identify stromal MTHFD2 as a redox-sensitive metabolic checkpoint linking fibrotic remodeling to immune evasion. Significance: Stromal MTHFD2 couples fibrotic remodeling to cGAS–STING-dependent inflammatory signaling and PD-L1 induction through redox-dependent cGAS–STING activation in lung cancer, creating a stromal niche that supports immune evasion.

papers.abstract: Abstract Allogeneic chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells could overcome limitations of autologous therapies but are limited by immune rejection. We evaluated 11 patients with large B-cell lymphoma treated with a single lot of cemacabtagene ansegedleucel (cema-cel), an allogeneic anti-CD19 CAR T product. Despite receiving identical infusion products (IP), patients exhibited heterogeneous cema-cel expansion and clinical outcomes. Our integrated analyses using longitudinal T-cell receptor (TCR) β sequencing, single-cell molecular profiling, and mixed lymphocyte reaction assays revealed that high frequencies of preexisting, recipient-derived alloreactive CD8+ T cells-mediated rapid CAR T rejection in nonexpanders. Furthermore, effector-like features, rather than stem/central memory programs, drove robust clonal CAR T expansion consistently across expanders. We confirmed similar expansion patterns in two independent cohorts treated with a separate lot of cema-cel or an allogeneic anti–B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) CAR T product. These findings highlight distinct cell-extrinsic and cell-intrinsic mechanisms that influence allogeneic CAR T performance and provide insights to optimize donor selection, manufacturing, and product design. Significance: Clinical adoption of allogeneic CAR T-cell therapies has been limited by poor CAR T-cell expansion in some recipients. Using patient samples, we elucidated the cell-extrinsic and cell-intrinsic mechanisms governing allogeneic CAR T-cell rejection and expansion. Our findings provide actionable strategies to improve allogeneic CAR T-cell efficacy.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Epigenetic silencing of tumour suppressor genes is a pivotal early event in colorectal cancer (CRC) pathogenesis. PDZ and LIM Domain 4 (PDLIM4) is a member of the PDZ‐LIM family with context‐dependent roles in tumour progression across different malignancies. However, its specific role and epigenetic regulation in colorectal cancer (CRC) remain elusive. Methods We integrated multi‐omics datasets and clinical cohorts to evaluate PDLIM4 expression and promoter methylation. Stool DNA was analyzed to assess the feasibility of non‐invasive detection of PDLIM4 promoter methylation. PDLIM4 knockout and overexpression cell lines were constructed to perform functional assays including proliferation, apoptosis, and stemness. In vivo experiments were validated utilizing xenograft mice or an azoxymethane (AOM)/ dextran sulphate sodium salt (DSS) CRC mouse model with intestinal epithelial cell‐specific overexpression of PDLIM4. Mechanistic investigations were conducted using coimmunoprecipitation coupled with mass spectrometry, RNA sequencing, ChIP‐qPCR and pharmacological rescue experiments. Results We identified a progressive loss of PDLIM4 protein along the normal‐adenoma‐carcinoma sequence, driven by DNMT3A‐mediated promoter hypermethylation, and lower PDLIM4 expression was associated with adverse patient prognosis. PDLIM4 methylation was also significantly increased in stool DNA from CRC patients compared with healthy controls. Mechanistically, genetic ablation of PDLIM4 significantly blunted the therapeutic efficacy of the DNA demethylating agent 5‐Azacytidine against CRC. Functionally, PDLIM4 restoration suppressed CRC cell proliferation and stemness while enhancing apoptosis in vitro, and reduced tumour growth in both AOM/DSS and xenograft models in vivo. At the molecular level, PDLIM4 interacted with BTF3 and promoted its autophagic‐lysosomal degradation, thereby limiting PI3K/Akt signalling, with NTRK2 identified as a potential transcriptional target linking BTF3 to PI3K/Akt activation. Conclusion DNMT3A‐mediated silencing of PDLIM4 is an early epigenetic event that facilitates CRC progression. PDLIM4 suppresses tumour growth by promoting BTF3 degradation, thereby restricting PI3K/Akt signalling. Thus, PDLIM4 methylation may have potential as a biomarker for early CRC detection. Key points DNMT3A‐mediated PDLIM4 promoter hypermethylation is an early event in colorectal tumorigenesis. Restoring PDLIM4 suppresses CRC proliferation and stemness while promoting apoptosis in vitro and in vivo. PDLIM4 promotes the autophagic‐lysosomal degradation of BTF3 and restrains PI3K/Akt signalling. Stool DNA analysis supports the potential of PDLIM4 methylation as a non‐invasive CRC biomarker

papers.abstract: Abstract Socioeconomic status (SES) is well recognized as an important determinant of cancer incidence and survival. However, its impact on outcomes in patients with mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) remains poorly characterized. We conducted a nationwide, population-based retrospective longitudinal study using German cancer registry data, including all patients diagnosed with MCL between 2013 and 2023. Regional SES was assessed annually at the district level using quintiles of the German Index of Socioeconomic Deprivation. The primary outcomes were 5-year absolute survival (AS) and relative survival (RS) as a proxy for disease-specific survival. A total of 8871 patients were included. Five-year AS and RS were 62.6% (95% CI, 61.5–63.7) and 72.1% (95% CI, 70.8–73.4), respectively. However, no meaningful differences in AS were observed between patients residing in districts of the lowest and highest SES quintiles (62.0% vs 63.1%). This nationwide population-based study indicates that regional socioeconomic deprivation was not associated with clinically relevant differences in survival outcomes among MCL patients in Germany between 2013 and 2023. These findings differ from previously described patterns in other lymphomas, suggesting that biological disease characteristics may exert a stronger influence on MCL survival than social determinants.

papers.abstract: Conventional MRI may not fully reflect the biological activity of vorasidenib. PET may detect treatment-related metabolic changes before structural changes become evident on MRI. We evaluated longitudinal PET and MRI changes in patients with IDH-mutant gliomas receiving vorasidenib. VORAFET is a longitudinal study of adults with IDH-mutant gliomas treated with vorasidenib. Eligible patients had predominantly non-enhancing WHO grade 2 or 3 gliomas, had not received prior radiotherapy or chemotherapy. The primary endpoint was longitudinal metabolic and structural imaging response according to PET RANO 1.0 and RANO 2.0. Integrated [¹⁸F]FET PET/MRI was performed at baseline and every 3 months. Thirty-nine patients were included; at baseline, 23 and 29 had PET and MRI-measurable disease. As best response, PET RANO 1.0 identified 2 complete and 12 partial responses, yielding an ORR of 60.9%; median time to first response was 4.5 months (range 3-12 months). RANO 2.0 showed no complete or partial responses, whereas 5 patients achieved minor response at a median of 9 months (range 6-12 months). Progressive disease occurred in 6 of 39 patients (15.4%) according to PET RANO 1.0 and in 1 of 39 (2.6%) according to RANO 2.0. Patients with PET-PD more often had subtle contrast enhancement and showed higher baseline FLAIR volume, MTV, TBRmax, and TBRmean. PET RANO 1.0 identified metabolic changes during vorasidenib treatment that were not always reflected by RANO 2.0 assessment. Longer follow-up is needed to clarify the relationship between PET metabolic changes and MRI findings and to determine their clinical significance.

papers.abstract: Abstract Adoptive T-cell therapies require T cells to sustain cytotoxic function for as long as tumor persists. In this issue, two independent studies converge on a ubiquitin-dependent pathway, centered on the cullin-5 (CUL5)–RING E3 ubiquitin ligase (CRL5) complex, as an intrinsic brake on T-cell function under repetitive antigen stimulation. Saco and colleagues demonstrate similar benefits with pharmacologic inhibition of CRL5 and related ubiquitin ligase complexes, whereas Bachl and colleagues extend the genetic benefit across multiple antigens and receptor architectures. Targeting this pathway offers a strategy to improve T-cell functional persistence and therapeutic durability. See related article by Bachl et al., p. XXX . See related article by Saco et al., p. papers.abstract: Postoperative stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT) is the standard adjuvant treatment after resection of brain metastases. It nevertheless requires delineation of a dynamic postsurgical cavity, delays local treatment by 3 to 6 weeks (and thus resumption of systemic therapy) and carries substantial risks of radiation necrosis and leptomeningeal disease. Preoperative SRT targets an intact lesion and may address some of these limitations. In this open-label, single-arm, multicenter phase 2 trial, eligible adults had a Karnofsky performance status ≥70 and up to four brain metastases, including one resectable lesion ≤5 cm, from breast, non-small cell lung, kidney, or digestive cancer or melanoma. Patients received preoperative SRT (three fractions of 7.7 Gy prescribed to the encompassing 70% isodose line, equivalent to 11Gy per fraction at the isocenter) followed by surgical resection within 3 days of the last fraction. The primary outcome was 6-month local control on centrally reviewed MRI. Secondary outcomes included index-lesion radiation necrosis, leptomeningeal disease, distant intracranial control, overall survival, toxicity, cognition, and quality of life. Of 73 patients assessed, 67 were eligible and 63 received both SRT and surgery. Median age was 62 years. At a median follow-up of 12.7 months, the 6-month local control rate was 100% (95% CI, 95%-100%), meeting the primary endpoint; the 12-month rate was 96.4% (95% CI, 87%-99%). No leptomeningeal disease occurred. The 1-year cumulative incidence of index-lesion radiation necrosis was 7% (95% CI, 2%-16%), meeting the key secondary endpoint. Distant intracranial failure occurred in 22 patients (35%); 12-month overall survival was 81.2% (95% CI, 70%-89%). Postoperative complications occurred in 4 patients (6.3%); cognition and quality of life remained stable over the 12 months of protocol follow-up. Three-fraction preoperative SRT followed by resection was associated with high local control, low radiation necrosis, and no leptomeningeal disease, supporting evaluation in ongoing randomized trials.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Survivors of childhood cancer (CCS) have higher risk of developing ischaemic heart disease (IHD), however, data on coronary anatomy, revascularisations, and prognosis remain limited. The objective was to investigate angiographic findings, invasive treatment patterns and mortality in CCS with IHD compared with controls without a history of childhood cancer. Methods This was a nationwide retrospective cohort-study of all 5-year survivors of leukaemia, lymphoma, or central nervous system cancer who subsequently developed IHD, with index cancer between 1958-2021. CCS were compared with population-based controls with IHD matched on cancer date by age, sex and residence. Results 136 CCS and 667 controls with IHD were included. CCS were a median of 5.2 years younger than controls at diagnosis of IHD. CCS had a higher prevalence of left main coronary artery (LMCA) stenosis (25.0% vs. 6.5%; p < 0.001) and multivessel disease (51.2% vs. 39.4%; p = 0.043). Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) was more frequently performed in CCS (22.8% vs. 11.4%; p < 0.001), although after adjusting for relevant covariates the difference was attenuated. After a median follow-up of 5.4 years following IHD diagnosis, CCS had higher hazard of all-cause mortality (HR 1.83, 95% CI 1.31-2.54; p < 0.001) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 2.04; 95% CI 1.42-2.95; p < 0.001). Conclusions CCS who developed IHD demonstrate a higher burden of extensive coronary artery disease, characterized by increased prevalence of LMCA stenosis and multivessel disease. Although overall revascularisation rates were similar, CCS experienced significantly higher all-cause and cardiovascular mortality following IHD-diagnosis compared with controls.

papers.abstract: Abstract Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells can provide cures to patients affected by certain hematologic malignancies. Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is a major side effect of this treatment, yet its pathophysiology remains incompletely understood and selective therapeutic options are limited. In this issue, Li and colleagues identify the CCR1–CCR2 axis as a key mediator of inflammatory macrophage recruitment to sites of CAR T-cell activation, thereby contributing to CRS. In preclinical models, blockade of this axis prevented macrophage recruitment and substantially diminished CRS severity. This discovery could open a new avenue for targeted intervention against CRS, although further validation of the role of the CCR1/CCR2 axis, particularly in clinically relevant settings, is required. papers.abstract: The efficacy of immunotherapy is commonly increased by simultaneous anti‐angiogenesis treatment. An experimental breast cancer model exhibits vascular normalization with reduced vascular leakage when grown in mice with endothelial Shb deficiency. This mutant ablates the effects of vascular endothelial growth factor A on angiogenesis and leakage. Unexpectedly, the endothelial gene expression changes that were observed under these conditions suggested an immunosuppressive state. Comparison of healthy human breast endothelium with breast cancer endothelium revealed similar immune suppressive gene expression differences, and lung cancer and colorectal cancer showed analogous patterns of changes. These findings suggest that normalized or physiologically normal endothelium may have immunosuppressive features, with implications for the optimization of cancer immunotherapy regimens.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Around 90% of children with cancer live in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs), with the majority dying of their disease. Despite the need for quality end‐of‐life (EoL) care in LMICs, access and integration remain limited. Quality indicators (QIs) can assess and provide standards for high‐quality care. The aim of this study was to develop QIs for EoL care for children diagnosed with cancer in LMICs. Methods The QIs were identified and prioritized through a multi‐phase process: (1) literature review identified potential QIs from existing guidelines, standards, and published studies; (2) modified Delphi approach engaged global experts to assess the importance and feasibility of QIs; and (3) prioritization conducted using a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) with experts and dot voting prioritization exercise with bereaved family members. Results From the literature review, 73 potential QIs were identified. Fifty‐six global experts from 27 countries participated in the modified Delphi. Sixty‐four indicators across seven domains were deemed important with 25 identified as both important and feasible. Forty‐one global experts from 23 countries participated in the DCE prioritization and 12 bereaved family members from nine countries participated in the dot voting prioritization. While experts and family members prioritized some indicators similarly (i.e., symptom management), family members placed higher priority on QIs addressing communication and anticipatory guidance. Conclusion This study describes a robust, context‐specific process which identified QIs for pediatric EoL care in LMICs. Future efforts will pilot and refine the QIs to demonstrate feasibility, sustainability, and impact on care quality. Precis This study assessed potential quality indicators (QIs) for pediatric end‐of‐life (EoL) care in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs) through a multi‐phase process involving global experts and bereaved families. The findings provide a set of potential QIs to evaluate and improve EoL care for children with cancer in LMICs.

papers.abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are integral components of the tumor microenvironment (TME) and are increasingly recognized as critical regulators of nearly every hallmark of cancer. Once viewed as a uniform, protumorigenic cell type, it is now clear that CAFs comprise a spectrum of dynamic and plastic functional states with both tumor-promoting and tumor-restraining capacities. This functional duality, conceptualized within the framework of cancer as a "wound that fails to heal", is dictated by their diverse cellular origins, the specific activation pathways engaged (such as TGF-β and PDGF), and the evolving cues from the TME. In this Review, we dissect the multifaceted roles of CAFs, from their promotion of cancer cell proliferation, invasion and angiogenesis through secreted factors and extensive extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, to their profound influence on the immune landscape. We detail how distinct CAF subsets, such as myofibroblastic (myCAFs) and inflammatory (iCAFs) CAFs, orchestrate an immunosuppressive niche and contribute to therapeutic resistance. We also explore the compelling evidence for tumor-suppressive CAF functions, which have catalyzed a paradigm shift in therapeutic strategies-moving away from indiscriminate CAF ablation towards nuanced approaches aimed at reprogramming their state. These strategies include modulating key signaling pathways, normalizing the CAF-remodeled ECM, and exploiting unique metabolic vulnerabilities. Finally, we discuss how advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics are resolving this complexity, paving the way for the development of precision therapies that can selectively neutralize pro-tumorigenic CAF activities while harnessing their beneficial functions to improve patient outcomes.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives. Pediatric brain tumor survivors (PBTS) are at increased risk of cardiometabolic complications due to tumor- and treatment-related hypothalamic–pituitary (HP) damage and adverse body composition. We evaluated associations of the Single-Point Insulin Sensitivity Estimator (SPISE) with central adiposity, DXA-derived body composition, metabolic abnormalities, and HP involvement. Methods. In this retrospective study, 119 PBTSs (median age, 12.7 years; median time since therapy, 2.4 years) were evaluated. SPISE, BMI, waist-to-height ratio (WHtR), DXA-derived fat-to-lean ratio (FLR), and metabolic syndrome (MetS) were assessed. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between SPISE and central adiposity. Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses compared the discriminatory performance of SPISE, BMI-SDS, HOMA-IR, and FLR. Results. Central adiposity was present in 58.8% of participants, whereas BMI-defined obesity occurred in 21.8%. Lower SPISE values were associated with central adiposity, obesity, MetS, HP damage, and multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies (all p < 0.05). SPISE declined across pubertal stages and remained associated with central adiposity after adjustment for age and selected HP variables (OR = 0.58, 95% CI 0.46–0.73). SPISE showed good discrimination of central adiposity (AUC = 0.81), with an exploratory, cohort-derived threshold of 7.82; FLR provided complementary information on body composition. Conclusions. Central adiposity was common and not fully captured by BMI-defined obesity. Lower SPISE values were associated with concurrent anthropometric and metabolic abnormalities, while DXA-derived FLR added descriptive information on body composition. Whether these indices improve cardiometabolic risk stratification beyond conventional measures requires prospective investigation.

papers.abstract: Tumor budding, defined as single tumor cells or clusters of up to four cells at the invasive front, is a morphological marker of tumor-cell dissociation and stromal invasion in colorectal cancer. Standardization by the International Tumor Budding Consensus Conference (ITBCC) established a reproducible hematoxylin-and-eosin-based method and enabled broader incorporation of budding into pathology reporting and clinical risk assessment. Intermediate- and high-grade budding are associated with lymph node metastasis in pT1 colorectal cancer, while high-grade budding identifies a subgroup of stage II colon cancers with increased recurrence risk. Adverse prognostic associations have also been reported in stage III disease and in rectal cancer after neoadjuvant therapy, although evidence that budding predicts benefit from a specific treatment is still insufficient. At the biological level, budding is linked to partial epithelial–mesenchymal transition, altered cell adhesion, cytoskeletal remodeling, and interactions with fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, and immune cells. Digital pathology and artificial intelligence may improve hotspot selection, quantification, and spatial characterization, but their clinical use depends on external validation, control of domain shift, and continued pathologist oversight. Tumor budding is therefore best interpreted as a complementary morphological biomarker alongside TNM stage, established histopathological risk factors, molecular features, and clinical context.
